extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and other practitioners who practice before the USPTO (particularly trademark practitioners) and participants in USPTO/OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing service, filing, signature/certification, representation, and sanctions in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (OED cases), with specific rules for trademark practice, TEAS signatures, and change-of-attorney filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of Complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director may serve a complaint by any method mutually agreeable to the OED Director and the respondent; other methods (e.g., sending to last known physical address) are available for unregistered respondents outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service via at least one mutually agreeable method satisfies Rule 11.35(a)(3). Evidence of receipt (e.g., the respondent's email reply or UPS tracking showing delivery) supports a finding of proper service. If a respondent has previously expressed a preference for email, serving by that email can be sufficient. When service by mutually agreeable method is established, the tribunal need not address alternative service methods (e.g., last known address under § 11.35(a)(4)(ii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely Filing of Answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An answer to a complaint must be filed within the time set in the complaint; in no event shall that time be less than thirty days from filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be timely, the answer must be filed by one of the methods specified in the complaint (see § 11.36(b) and the complaint's instructions). Failure to file an answer within the required time constitutes an admission of the allegations and may lead to default judgment under § 11.36(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Method and Place for Filing an Answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An answer 'shall be filed in writing with the hearing officer at the address specified in the complaint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible filing methods will be specified in the complaint (e.g., U.S. mail/commercial delivery to OALJ physical address or electronic filing via the OALJ E-Filing System). Informal delivery (e.g., emailing a copy to the Headquarters Hearing Clerk) does not constitute effective filing unless expressly permitted; parties must follow the complaint/OSPP filing instructions and may seek filing assistance from provided contacts if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default Consequences for Failure to File Answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer to a complaint will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a respondent is found in default, the hearing officer may deem all well-pled factual allegations admitted and proceed to determine violations and appropriate sanctions based on those admitted facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and Standard of Proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director has the burden of proving alleged disciplinary violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence requires proof that produces a firm belief or conviction, i.e., a level of proof between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt. Evidence should be certain, unambiguous, and persuasive enough to convince the trier of fact without hesitancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Authority and Procedural Rules for Discipline (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D), 32; 37 C.F.R. Part 11 Subpart C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for practice before it and to suspend or exclude practitioners; disciplinary proceedings are conducted under the Procedural Rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19–11.60) and afford notice and opportunity for hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary authority includes promulgating rules of professional conduct and conducting proceedings consistent with the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 556). Hearing officers are appointed pursuant to applicable statutes and regs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Scope of 'Practice Before the Office' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Practice before the Office' includes law-related services connected with presenting matters to the Office relating to a client's rights, privileges, duties, or responsibilities under laws or regulations administered by the Office (explicitly including preparing or prosecuting trademark applications and related documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-attorneys who do not meet § 11.14 may not prepare applications or represent applicants/registrants in USPTO trademark matters (see TMEP § 608.01). The designation of what activities constitute practice is broad and includes prosecution, amendments requiring written argument, and filings affecting registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule for Foreign-Domiciled Trademark Applicants (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a); § 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant, registrant, or party whose domicile is not within the United States or its territories must be represented by an attorney qualified under § 11.14 (a U.S.-licensed attorney or approved reciprocal recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Counsel Rule seeks to ensure U.S. registrations issued to foreign applicants comply with signature and use requirements and to enable enforcement of compliance. Foreign-domiciled applicants cannot be represented by non-U.S attorneys except as authorized by the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner Certification Requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a)–(b); § 11.18(b)(2) elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every practitioner who presents a document to the USPTO must certify to the best of their knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, that (i) the paper is not for improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument; (iii) factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after reasonable opportunity for investigation/discovery; and (iv) denials are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must make reasonable inquiry before certifying; false statements can have serious consequences (declarations for trademark use also are sworn and subject to 18 U.S.C. § 1001). Presenting documents without adequate inquiry (e.g., using pre-dated declarations that do not support the submission) violates § 11.18.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS Signature Methods and Proper Use (DIRECT and H-SIGN)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trademark Electronic Application System (TEAS) permits multiple signature methods including DIRECT (the originator signs directly via TEAS shortly before filing) and H-SIGN (a scanned handwritten pen-and-ink signature is submitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H-SIGN involves creating an electronic file of a handwritten signature (typically printing and physically signing). Using previously executed handwritten declarations (pre-signed H-SIGN files) to support unrelated later filings—so that the declaration predates the Office Action or specimen it purports to verify—undermines the § 11.18 certification and is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature Requirements and Prohibition on Others Signing (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: All documents requiring a signature must be personally signed or have the signature personally entered by the named signatory; another person (paralegal, assistant, secretary) may not sign or enter the name of a qualified U.S. attorney or other authorized signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to physical and electronic signatures. Typing or inserting another person's electronic signature does not constitute that person's valid signature. Case law (e.g., In re Dermahose, In re Cowan) supports strict adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change-of-Attorney / Change of Representation Rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.17, 2.18; TMEP § 604.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the USPTO recognizes a qualified U.S. attorney as representative, a new qualified U.S. attorney from a different firm may not represent the applicant/registrant until: (1) the applicant revokes the previous power of attorney; (2) the applicant submits a new power of attorney naming the new attorney; (3) recognition of the previous attorney is deemed ended under § 2.17(g); or (4) the previous attorney withdraws or is suspended/excluded. The revocation/new power must be signed by the applicant or someone authorized to bind the applicant; the new attorney may not sign the revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until such formal action is taken, the new attorney cannot sign responses, authorize amendments, change correspondence address, or otherwise act as representative. Improperly signed CAR forms or unauthorized attorney-of-record filings can result in Non-Responsive Submissions, refusals, delays, and abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Cooperate with OED Investigations (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.801(b), 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are required to cooperate with the USPTO's disciplinary investigations and to respond to requests for information (RFIs) from OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to RFIs or otherwise to cooperate can constitute a violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct and is treated as an aggravating factor when determining sanctions (e.g., bad faith obstruction by intentional noncompliance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Actual and Potential Client Harm in Sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining sanctions, the tribunal considers whether the respondent's misconduct caused actual or potential harm to clients; harm is not required to establish an RPC violation but is relevant to sanction severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of harm include delays in prosecution, additional fees, and abandoned applications (e.g., where improper signatures led to denial and eventual abandonment). Demonstrated harm or significant risk of harm supports a heightened sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and Mitigating Factors (ABA Standards § 9.0; used with 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunals routinely consider ABA Standards' lists of aggravating and mitigating factors in selecting sanctions; cited aggravating factors include dishonest or selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, and bad faith obstruction; mitigating factors can include absence of a prior disciplinary record and timely good-faith efforts to make restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors such as intentional misconduct, patterns across multiple clients or filings, persistence despite notice, and failure to comply with orders counsel in favor of suspension or exclusion. Limited mitigation (e.g., no prior record) may not overcome serious aggravation. The tribunal exercises broad discretion under § 11.20 and applies § 11.54(b)'s factors in imposing sanctions (e.g., suspension with probation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of Well-Pled Allegations upon Default
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent defaults under § 11.36(e), their failure to answer constitutes an admission of all well-pled factual allegations in the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those admitted facts can be the basis for findings of violation and for determining sanctions without further factual development. Default is thus procedural and substantive in effect insofar as it simplifies the proving of facts in the complaint.
